reviewBoundary: Eight explicitly authored original complete paired-reading practices. Each group has two full passages with five four-option questions each; frozen originals provide level and task structure only. Same-author entailment, unique-key and all-distractor audit, not independent teacher/learner calibration, official CET provenance, publication or production approval.

units.title: 四级阅读：面包表面的褐变与玻璃瓶中的水滴

materials.title: More Than One Way to Turn Brown
materials.text:
A bakery class compared two pieces of bread from the same dough. One had a dark crust and a soft middle; the other had remained pale under a different heating arrangement. A student suggested that the brown surface was simply bread becoming dry, so any equally dry piece must eventually look and taste the same.

The tutor explained that losing water and developing colour were related in the baking conditions but were not identical processes. Water could leave a surface without producing every chemical change associated with a browned crust. The temperature, time and available substances mattered as well. A dry piece left in a cool room did not therefore reproduce the complete history of a baked surface.

One important set of browning reactions involved substances from sugars and amino compounds. Their products could contribute both colour and aroma. The lesson distinguished this from the idea that all brown food had been coloured by one universal reaction. Other ingredients and processes could also create brown appearances, and a visible shade did not identify the complete chemistry of an unknown sample.

The surface and the middle did not experience identical conditions. While much water remained in the middle, its temperature history differed from that of the exposed crust. The class compared these locations rather than reporting one oven setting as the temperature of every point in the loaf throughout baking.

For its records, the group kept sample position, heating arrangement and observation time with the photographs. It did not make a judgement about flavour from colour alone. Two pieces could look similar while differing in moisture, texture or the combination of aromas produced. The practical lesson was to connect an appearance with its conditions and the question being asked. Brownness could be useful evidence, but it was not a complete account of what had happened to the bread.

questions.prompt: Why was the student’s explanation incomplete?
options: Any dry bread necessarily had the same aroma.
Drying and browning were not identical processes with interchangeable conditions.
The tutor said bread could never lose water.
Brown colour always came from an added dye.
questions.explanation: B正确：失水与褐变相关但不同，还取决温时和物质。A相反；C明说水可离开；D未认全为染料。

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about the browning reactions discussed?
options: They were the only possible cause of brown food.
They made the ingredients irrelevant.
They occurred identically in every cool room.
They could involve sugars and amino compounds and contribute colour and aroma.
questions.explanation: D正确：糖与氨基化合物参与，产物可给色香。A否认通一反应；C冷干不等烤；B物质条件重要。

questions.prompt: Why compare the crust and the middle?
options: Their exposure and water conditions could give them different temperature histories.
Only the middle could contain any water.
They necessarily had identical temperatures at every moment.
The oven setting directly measured each point in the loaf.
questions.explanation: A正确：中部留水与外露表面条件异，不能炉设当各点全时温。C、D正是排除误解；B非仅中有水。

questions.prompt: Why keep conditions with the photographs?
options: To replace every description with a colour ranking.
To prove that taste could be read perfectly from images.
To link the visible result with where, when and how the sample was heated.
To show that position never mattered.
questions.explanation: C正确：记录位置加热安排观察时供外观关联条件。A没取代描述；B色不定味；D位置须记。

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Similar brownness does not ensure identical moisture, texture or aroma.
Every pale loaf has exactly the same chemical history.
Colour is useless in any food observation.
One oven setting makes every part of bread identical.
questions.explanation: A正确：末段同色可异水分质地香组合，色非全史。B无据；C只限定非无用；D表里不同。

materials.title: Water inside a Closed Glass Garden
materials.text:
A college display contained small plants and soil in a transparent closed container. Drops appeared on the glass and later became less visible. A visitor assumed that every new drop must mean someone had opened the lid and watered the plants while nobody was watching.

The gardener explained that water already inside the container could move among soil, plants, air and surfaces. Liquid could enter the air as water vapour. Plant leaves could also release water into the surrounding air through their normal processes. When a surface was sufficiently cool under the relevant conditions, some vapour could become liquid on it. A visible drop could therefore be part of an internal movement rather than evidence of a new external addition.

The closed lid limited exchange with the room; it did not stop every process inside. Light and heat could still pass through or interact with the container. Calling the system closed for water exchange did not mean that nothing entered or left in any form. The display label stated which kind of boundary it meant.

Nor did the repeated appearance of drops prove that conditions were suitable for every possible plant forever. The balance of light, temperature, available water and the plants’ requirements still mattered. The gardener described the particular maintained display and kept its history, rather than treating one attractive container as a universal design for a self-managing garden.

Students recorded where and when drops were seen. A single dry-looking patch of glass did not show that the whole system contained no water. Equally, a heavily misted wall did not reveal the exact amount available to every root. The observations offered clues about movements and conditions, not a direct reading of every internal store.

The container thus made an ordinary process visible: water could change location and state without being newly created. Understanding the route was more informative than inventing an unseen watering event whenever a drop appeared.

questions.prompt: What alternative explains new drops without opening the lid?
options: Water was newly created by the glass.
The plants had stopped every internal process.
Water inside could enter the air and later become liquid on a cooler surface.
All drops necessarily came from room air passing through an open lid.
questions.explanation: C正确：内部水入气相后遇适冷表面凝成液，不需新外加。A非创水；B仍有过程；D不必开盖。

questions.prompt: What does the passage mean by a closed boundary?
options: The stated boundary concerned water exchange and did not mean all processes ceased.
Every kind of exchange was impossible.
No light or heat could interact with the container.
All plants inside had identical needs.
questions.explanation: A正确：限水交换非一切物能交换，更非内部停。C、B扩大closed；D未说需求同。

questions.prompt: Why is one successful display insufficient as a universal gardening design?
options: Drops prove every root always has enough water.
The lid removes the role of temperature.
Plant requirements cease after the first day.
Its maintained conditions and particular plants do not establish suitability for every plant forever.
questions.explanation: D正确：特定维护史及光温水需求未可外推永久全植物。A滴不量根水；B温重要；C需求仍在。

questions.prompt: What can a dry-looking patch of glass establish?
options: The absence of all water in soil and plants.
Only a local appearance, rather than the absence of water throughout the system.
Proof that the lid had been opened.
The exact amount of water at every root.
questions.explanation: B正确：一小片干只局部所见，不能量全系统或各根水。A、D越证据；C不证开盖。

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the account?
options: To claim that water is created whenever glass cools.
To show that a closed garden can never need maintenance.
To explain visible drops through movements and state changes of existing water.
To infer every internal condition from one photograph.
questions.explanation: C正确：末段以位置相态过程解释既有水，胜于凭滴猜外加。A否定创水；B维护案例；D外观只线索。

units.title: 四级阅读：慈善竞拍的出价与舞台道具的可读性

materials.title: The Bid That Was Not Yet a Donation
materials.text:
A student society held a fictional charity auction. Its online page showed the highest bid beside each offered item. Before the event ended, a volunteer added all those figures and announced that the money had already reached the charity.

The organiser corrected the announcement. A bid was a stated offer under the auction’s rules. The eventual winning bidder would still need to complete payment through the announced process. An item could fail to reach its stated condition for sale, a bid could be withdrawn where the rules allowed, or a payment might not be completed. The current leading offer was useful information, but it was not the same event as money being received.

The society therefore kept several amounts distinct. It recorded accepted sales, payments actually received and costs that had to be deducted before the stated net donation. A headline total of successful bids and a final transfer to the charity answered different accounting questions. They could both be accurately reported if their labels and dates were clear.

Some supporters also gave money without bidding on any item. These direct gifts were recorded through a separate route so they were not accidentally counted once as a payment and again as an extra donation. The organiser explained that a clear distinction need not make a report complicated: a short table could identify each stage and its meaning.

The final announcement included the amount transferred, the date and a brief explanation of how it related to the earlier auction figures. It did not describe an unpaid promise as cash already delivered. Nor did it treat a useful preliminary estimate as dishonest merely because the final figure differed. The lesson was about the status of a number. Before asking whether the total was large, the volunteers needed to ask what had been counted, at which stage, and for which purpose.

questions.prompt: What was wrong with the volunteer’s first announcement?
options: It refused all direct gifts.
It reported any interest in the event.
It distinguished offered amounts from payments.
It treated current bids as if the corresponding money had already been received by the charity.
questions.explanation: D正确：最高出价是报价状态，不等已收并转慈善钱。B可报兴趣；C原错误恰未区分；A没拒礼。

questions.prompt: Why could the final transfer differ from the headline bid total?
options: Every bidder necessarily paid twice.
Sale conditions, completed payments and relevant deductions affected the stages counted.
A leading bid was always the same as a completed transfer.
The passage said no records were kept.
questions.explanation: B正确：成交条件、付款完成及应扣成本使竞价额异净转款。A无双付规则；C错误；D各阶段有记。

questions.prompt: Why record direct gifts separately?
options: To prevent donors from supporting the charity.
To make all gifts disappear from the report.
To avoid counting the same money through two routes.
To guarantee every auction item sold.
questions.explanation: C正确：直接捐赠另路防一笔当付款又当额外捐款。A、B反目的；D不保竞品全售。

questions.prompt: How does the organiser regard a preliminary estimate?
options: As potentially useful if its counted stage and limitations are clear.
As proof all payments are complete.
As a substitute for every dated record.
As necessarily dishonest whenever it differs from the final number.
questions.explanation: A正确：早估数有用但要标阶段日期，异终额不自动骗人。D极端；B未付款；C仍需记录。

questions.prompt: What question should precede judging the size of a total?
options: Whether the largest bid came first alphabetically.
What it counts, at which stage and for what purpose.
Whether every item used the same photograph.
How to erase an earlier accurate estimate.
questions.explanation: B正确：末段计什么、何阶段、用途先明。A、C文无此要求；D早版可准确留解释非抹。

materials.title: A Letter Seen from the Back Row
materials.text:
A theatre group made a letter that an actor would open on stage. The first prop reproduced a realistic private note, with tiny handwriting and a pale envelope. Up close, it looked convincing. During rehearsal, however, people at the back of the room could not recognise the moment when the actor discovered an important mark on it.

The designer asked what the audience needed to understand. They did not have to read every sentence of the imaginary letter. They needed to see that a particular mark had caught the character’s attention and changed the scene. Making the complete text larger would not automatically solve that specific problem.

The group tested the prop from relevant seats under the actual rehearsal lighting. A stronger difference between the mark and its background helped, as did a change in how the actor held the paper. The team treated material, light, angle and timing as a connected arrangement. A photograph taken at the worktable could not establish how the prop would function during the scene.

The actor also needed an object that could be handled consistently. A fragile sheet that looked excellent in one still view might fail when opened repeatedly. The group therefore kept visual effect and practical use in the same test, rather than choosing a prop solely because it was impressive in isolation.

For a later performance in another room, the designer retained the purpose of the mark but checked the arrangement again. A larger room or different light could change what was visible. Keeping the same story function did not require preserving every physical detail unchanged.

The final letter was less like an ordinary personal note when examined closely, yet it communicated the intended event more clearly in performance. The result did not prove that realism was always wrong. It showed that a theatrical object needed to be judged in the situation where its audience and performer would use it.

questions.prompt: What specific problem did the first prop have?
options: The important mark and the actor’s discovery were unclear from distant seats.
Its complete text was required to be read by every viewer.
The actor was forbidden to hold any paper.
No audience member could see the stage at all.
questions.explanation: A正确：后排看不明注意到标记这一戏剧时刻，非全信须读。B反文；C、D无据。

questions.prompt: Why was enlarging every sentence not necessarily sufficient?
options: The letter contained no words.
All props had to be smaller than real notes.
Lighting could never affect printed material.
The audience’s key task was to recognise a meaningful mark, not read the whole letter.
questions.explanation: D正确：剧情需看标记引反应，全体文本变大未必针对它。A原有细字；B无定规；C光影响。

questions.prompt: What did testing under rehearsal conditions reveal?
options: Only the worktable photograph mattered.
Contrast, holding angle, light and timing contributed together to the effect.
Every seat had the same view by definition.
Handling was unrelated to performance.
questions.explanation: B正确：材质光角时及对比共同构效果，还需可反复操作。A否定；D需操作；C不同座核。

questions.prompt: Why check the prop again in a new room?
options: The character’s story had to be erased.
Every previous decision had necessarily been dishonest.
The same story function could require a different physical arrangement under changed conditions.
An unchanged object always communicates identically everywhere.
questions.explanation: C正确：功能可保而房间光空间变需重核物理细节。B无此；A不需抹剧情；D否定普同。

questions.prompt: Which principle does the outcome illustrate?
options: A prop’s success depends on its use in the performance context.
Realistic props can never be useful.
The closest viewer is the only audience that matters.
Durability automatically makes a prop readable.
questions.explanation: A正确：道具要在观演操作情境评，不判所有写实错。B极端；C需后排；D耐用可读不同。

units.title: 四级阅读：可触摸复制件的用途与游戏教程的学习顺序

materials.title: A Copy Visitors Could Touch
materials.text:
A local museum displayed a fragile carved object inside a case. Beside it, a newly made replica allowed visitors to explore the shape by touch. After handling the copy, a visitor said the original must have exactly the same surface because the outline appeared identical.

The curator explained how the replica had been made and what it was intended to communicate. It reproduced selected dimensions and major carved features. Its material, finish and method of production differed from those of the historical object. The copy could therefore help explain the arrangement of the carving without serving as direct evidence of every original surface property.

The label named the copied features and the differences relevant to touch. Visitors were invited to compare the broad form, but not told that a smooth modern finish proved how the old object had felt when new. The original had its own material history, including use and later treatment. A recent copy could not silently replace that history.

For a visitor unable to inspect the object visually, the replica offered an important route into its structure. The curator did not dismiss that route because it was selective. Every display method selected some information: a photograph also depended on angle, light and what had been placed in view. The useful question was which information each method made available and how its limits were explained.

The museum kept the replica clearly identified and recorded later changes to it. When a damaged part was replaced, the new piece was not presented as additional evidence discovered in the original. The display remained useful because its relationship to the object could be followed.

Touching the copy was thus an encounter with a carefully designed interpretation. It expanded access while keeping the historical object distinct. A copy did not need to be identical in every respect to be informative, but the information it offered needed an honest description of what had actually been reproduced.

questions.prompt: Why could the replica not prove every original surface property?
options: Every visitor had handled the original.
The curator said the replica had no shape.
It used different materials, finish and production while reproducing selected features.
Its label claimed every surface was identical.
questions.explanation: C正确：仿尺寸大特征但材质工法表面异，不证全原触感。B可表形；A原在柜；D标签明差。

questions.prompt: What should the smooth modern finish not be taken to establish?
options: Exactly how the historical object felt when it was new.
That the copy existed.
That some structural information was accessible.
That visitors could handle the replica.
questions.explanation: A正确：现代光面不证原物初成触感，原物另有史。B、C、D都是既明事实非所禁推论。

questions.prompt: How does the curator regard selective access through the copy?
options: As worthless because it is selective.
As a complete replacement for the original’s history.
As proof photographs contain every possible detail.
As useful when the information and limits of the method are explained.
questions.explanation: D正确：选择性不等无用，各媒介选信息，要明可用与限。A反文；B不换历史；C照片亦选。

questions.prompt: Why record replacements made to the replica?
options: To pretend new copy parts were discovered in the original.
To preserve a traceable account of what the copy represented and how it changed.
To show that the original was newly manufactured.
To make its label disappear.
questions.explanation: B正确：副本身份及后改留记录，免新件伪原证。A正要避免；D要标签；C原不变新。

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main argument?
options: Every copy automatically preserves original material history.
Only a copy identical in every respect can teach anything.
An informative copy may reproduce selected features if its relation to the original is clear.
Touch provides no information about shape.
questions.explanation: C正确：复制不需全同才有教益，但实际复制何物须诚实。B极端；A不能自动承原史；D可触形。

materials.title: The Tutorial after the Easy Level
materials.text:
A student game club tested a puzzle game with newcomers. Its tutorial began with a long list of controls, special cases and scoring rules. Experienced members considered it clear because every rule could be found somewhere in the explanation. Several newcomers, however, forgot which control mattered when they met their first puzzle.

The designer watched where they hesitated. Some had understood the words but had no immediate opportunity to connect them with an action. The club tried introducing one basic move in a simple situation, then adding another rule when the next puzzle made it relevant. This did not mean hiding a condition until after a player had been unfairly penalised. Information needed for a decision still had to be available before that decision.

The new sequence improved completion of the opening puzzles in the club’s small test. The designer nevertheless kept that result separate from mastery of the whole game. A player might succeed by following a visible prompt without remembering the rule when the prompt disappeared. The club therefore included a later opportunity to use the move with less assistance.

Feedback also needed care. A message saying wrong gave little help when several actions could have caused the failure. The revised version connected feedback with the relevant move and showed what the player could reconsider. It did not supply the entire solution automatically whenever a learner paused.

The club retained an accessible route to the full rules for players who wanted to consult them. Sequencing the first encounter did not remove the value of a complete reference. The two forms served different moments in learning.

The designer’s conclusion was modest: the tested sequence helped these newcomers begin under these conditions. Further stages and different players still needed attention. A successful tutorial was not simply the shortest explanation or the longest list. It connected timely information, action, feedback and later independent use.

questions.prompt: Why was a complete list insufficient for some newcomers?
options: They were required to memorise no rules.
They could understand words without connecting the relevant rule to their first action.
The game had no controls.
Experienced players were unable to read the tutorial.
questions.explanation: B正确：全列但新手无当下行动关联，开局忘所需控。A无此禁记；C有控；D老手认为清。

questions.prompt: What limited the claim based on easier opening completion?
options: It proved mastery of every later puzzle.
It showed that prompts were never used.
Prompted success did not necessarily establish later independent use.
It made every further observation unnecessary.
questions.explanation: C正确：跟提示成功未必移除后会用，后设少助任务。A、D过推；B有提示。

questions.prompt: How was feedback improved?
options: It connected the difficulty with a move the player could reconsider.
It always revealed the complete solution immediately.
It appeared only after the whole game ended.
It called every action wrong without explanation.
questions.explanation: A正确：关联相关动作供重想，非停顿即全解。D原问题；B否定；C没延到结尾。

questions.prompt: Why keep a full-rule reference?
options: It replaced all opportunities to practise.
It guaranteed every learner would memorise it at once.
It allowed necessary conditions to be hidden until after penalties.
It served consultation needs alongside the sequenced first encounter.
questions.explanation: D正确：完整查阅和分步初学各有时机。B不保全记；C应决策前可得；A仍需练。

questions.prompt: What conclusion did the designer support?
options: The sequence was universally best for all players.
It helped the tested newcomers begin, while further learning and different users still needed checks.
The shortest tutorial must always be best.
A long rule list is the only valid teaching method.
questions.explanation: B正确：限定这些新人此条件开局效，后阶段与别人仍需核。A普推；C、D单一长度准则均拒。

units.title: 四级阅读：声音漫步的方向判断与遗址发掘的取样边界

materials.title: The Loudest Sound Was Not the Nearest
materials.text:
A class took a fictional sound walk using a prepared set of observations. At one position, a distant engine sounded louder than a nearby stream. A student concluded that their ears had proved the engine was closer, since sound became quieter with distance.

The tutor agreed that distance could affect a sound reaching a listener, but pointed out the missing comparison. The two sources did not begin with the same strength. Their sound also travelled through different surroundings. A stronger source farther away could reach the listener more loudly than a weaker one nearby. Received loudness alone did not isolate distance when other conditions differed.

Direction presented another question. A wall could reflect sound, making the apparent route to a listener different from a direct line to the source. The class recorded the position and nearby surfaces before treating an impression as a precise location. A useful listening report could say what was heard and where without claiming a complete map of every source.

The exercise also separated a continuous sound from a brief event. A short observation might miss an occasional bell even though it was part of the area’s daily sound pattern. Absence during one interval was not evidence that the bell had never sounded there. Conversely, hearing it once did not show that it rang throughout the day.

The group compared records taken over stated periods. It did not replace every listener’s description with one number, because source identity, timing and direction could matter as well as level. Nor did it assume that a measurement made for one purpose answered every question about comfort or the experience of a place.

The final record was a situated account of listening. It became stronger when it named conditions and uncertainty, rather than turning one striking sound into a complete explanation of the surrounding environment.

questions.prompt: Why did louder received sound not prove the engine was closer?
options: The sources differed in strength and transmission conditions as well as distance.
Distance can never affect sound.
The stream had been proven silent.
All sources emitted the same sound by definition.
questions.explanation: A正确：声源原强和传播环境异，耳处响度未隔离距离。B距离可影响；C溪有声；D非同源强。

questions.prompt: Why note a nearby wall?
options: It made every measurement exact.
It guaranteed the source was behind the listener.
Reflection could affect the apparent direction of the sound.
It prevented every sound from reaching the class.
questions.explanation: C正确：墙反射可改抵耳路线和表观向，记录表面免当直线源位。A不保精；B无固定方；D仍闻。

questions.prompt: What can a short interval without a bell establish?
options: That the bell has never existed.
Only that it was not heard in that interval, subject to the observation conditions.
That it rang all day.
That the engine and stream had identical source strength.
questions.explanation: B正确：短时无闻限时条件，非永无，闻一次也非全天。A、C越范围；D无关。

questions.prompt: Why retain descriptions alongside levels?
options: Numbers could never be useful.
Every sound question concerned loudness alone.
Source identity was always obvious from one number.
Timing, direction and source identity could answer questions that level alone did not.
questions.explanation: D正确：级量以外还有身份时向，各用途不同，非数字全问。A未否数；B、C过简化。

questions.prompt: What strengthens the final sound record?
options: Stating listening conditions and the limits of what was inferred.
Calling every impression an exact source map.
Erasing observation periods.
Assuming one sound explains the whole place.
questions.explanation: A正确：情境记录明条件不确定，非一突出声全环境。B不精确全图；C保时段；D正排。

materials.title: The Square That Was Left Unexcavated
materials.text:
A fictional archaeology team investigated part of an old settlement. Its first display showed a small excavated square containing several broken vessels. A visitor asked why the team had not dug every surrounding area immediately, since more digging must always produce a better account.

The archaeologist explained that excavation changed the place being studied. Removing a layer could reveal information, but the original arrangement could not simply be put back after the work. Careful records preserved aspects of it; they did not make every physical relationship recoverable forever. The team therefore treated the decision to excavate as a choice requiring a question and an appropriate method.

Some surrounding ground remained unexcavated so other evidence and future methods could still be considered. This did not mean the team knew it contained nothing. Non-invasive observations could also guide questions, although they had their own limits and were not equivalent to opening the ground.

The small square was a sample of a larger area. Its finds supported claims about that location and could suggest wider questions. They did not establish that the same objects occurred with identical frequency everywhere in the settlement. The report named how the square had been selected and what was beyond its coverage.

Within it, the position and relationships of fragments mattered. A vessel found in a later disturbed layer did not necessarily belong to the earliest use of the building simply because its style looked old. The team considered the context as well as the object’s appearance.

The public account therefore included what had been examined, what remained and why. A complete story was not created merely by removing more ground. Better knowledge depended on a connection between the question, the material, the method and the record, together with a clear statement of what the evidence did not yet settle.

questions.prompt: Why was excavation described as a consequential choice?
options: Every removed layer could be restored exactly without records.
The team had no research question.
It never supplied any useful evidence.
It could reveal information while irreversibly changing original physical arrangements.
questions.explanation: D正确：开层得证也改变原关系，记录不能全物理复原。A反文；C可供证；B需问题。

questions.prompt: What did leaving some ground unexcavated mean?
options: The team had proved it empty.
It preserved possibilities for other evidence and future methods without claiming emptiness.
It had no possible future value.
All non-invasive methods were identical to digging.
questions.explanation: B正确：保未来方法及他证选择，不等知空，无损法亦有限非同挖。A、C错；D明异。

questions.prompt: Why explain selection of the excavated square?
options: To make its contents automatically representative of every area.
To erase the local findings.
To show what the sample covered and limit wider generalisation.
To avoid recording its location.
questions.explanation: C正确：明抽样位置及界，局部物频不等全村相同。A过推；B保发现；D要定位。

questions.prompt: Why could an old-looking vessel fail to date the building’s earliest use?
options: Its disturbed later context could differ from the time suggested by its style.
Style always precisely dated every building.
All fragments were modern plastic.
The team treated context as irrelevant.
questions.explanation: A正确：旧样器在后扰层不必属最初使用，需位置关系。B绝对；C无据；D语境重要。

questions.prompt: What does the passage favour over simply digging more?
options: Refusing all investigation.
Treating every small sample as a complete settlement history.
Counting objects without their positions.
Matching questions, methods, context and records while stating what remains uncertain.
questions.explanation: D正确：末段问题材料方法记录连结并明未定，非挖越多自好。A未拒研究；C需位置；B拒全推。

units.title: 六级阅读：地下水位恢复与手稿识读的不确定性

materials.title: When the Water Rose but the Ground Did Not
materials.text:
A fictional basin study compared groundwater records with measurements of land movement. After pumping declined, water levels rose in several observation wells. A summary announced that the land must therefore have returned to its previous height. The research team separated recovery of a water-level measurement from reversal of changes in the material surrounding the aquifer.

Groundwater pressure could help support part of the load carried within a sediment system. When pumping changed that pressure, stresses within compressible layers could change too. Some deformation might be recoverable, while other compaction could leave a persistent reduction in volume under the conditions considered. Reintroducing water did not automatically restore the earlier arrangement of particles. A rising well measurement and a complete rebound of the ground were therefore different propositions.

The basin was not a single uniform block. Layers differed in their permeability and mechanical properties. A pressure change recorded quickly in one location could reach another layer more slowly. The timing of surface movement might consequently differ from the timing of the water-level response in a selected well. A neat pair of annual endpoints could conceal continuing adjustment between the observations.

The team linked the instruments to what they actually measured. A well represented conditions at its screened interval, not every depth beneath the town. A land-motion measurement concerned displacement relative to its stated reference. Comparing the records required attention to place, depth, time and measurement uncertainty, rather than treating two instruments with different targets as competing answers to exactly the same question.

Other processes could also influence land height. The analysis considered the relevant background movement and local changes before assigning every measured displacement to pumping. That did not make the groundwater mechanism unimportant. It made a causal claim require evidence about the alternatives and the connection between pressure changes and deformation.

The practical assessment therefore retained both water and land records. Reduced pumping could be beneficial even if it did not undo every past change. Conversely, a short period without obvious surface movement did not guarantee that no delayed response remained. The report avoided the symmetrical errors of equating water recovery with complete physical restoration and dismissing recovery because restoration was incomplete.

Its central result was methodological: the meaning of recovery depends on which state is being measured and which earlier condition is the reference. A policy could improve one part of a coupled system without making its entire history reversible. Evaluating it required a description of the changed quantities, their relationships and the timescale over which the evidence had been collected.

questions.prompt: Why did rising well levels not establish complete restoration of land height?
options: Water measurements and land measurements were identical by definition.
Some compaction could persist after pressure recovered.
No sediment could ever deform.
The report stated that particles always returned to exactly their earlier arrangement.
questions.explanation: B正确：有些压密不可完全回复，水压升不使粒序和地高自动回原。A测量对象异；C可变形；D明不保。

questions.prompt: What role did differences among layers play?
options: They guaranteed an instantaneous uniform response everywhere.
They proved all surface motion came from one cause.
They made well depth irrelevant.
They could produce different pressure and deformation responses over time.
questions.explanation: D正确：渗透和力学异使压力传达时延与地动时间不同。A反；C须深度；B仍核他因。

questions.prompt: Why identify a well’s screened interval?
options: To claim it measured every layer simultaneously.
To replace displacement measurements with rainfall totals.
To locate the conditions represented by its water-level record.
To eliminate every form of uncertainty automatically.
questions.explanation: C正确：井记录限筛段，标深位才知代表何处非全深。A扩大；B非降雨替代；D不消全疑。

questions.prompt: How should incomplete physical reversal affect assessment of reduced pumping?
options: It does not by itself erase benefits, but it limits claims of complete restoration.
It guarantees all delayed responses have ended.
It makes both kinds of record unnecessary.
It proves the intervention had no possible benefit.
questions.explanation: A正确：减抽可益且旧变未全逆，两误区都避，仍双记录和时程。D否益；B不保迟效完；C仍需。

questions.prompt: What does the passage’s account of recovery require?
options: Assuming improvement in one variable reverses every change.
Using a single endpoint as a complete history.
Specifying the measured state, reference condition, relationships and timescale.
Treating instruments with different targets as exactly interchangeable.
questions.explanation: C正确：末段恢复须定变量参照关系与时标，单部改善非全史逆转。B端点隐中程；A、D反主张。

materials.title: The Letter That Software Could Not Quite Read
materials.text:
A fictional archive tested handwriting-recognition software on personal notebooks. The system produced searchable text quickly, but some uncertain words appeared as ordinary confident sentences. A project manager suggested displaying only the most likely output, reasoning that readers wanted smooth prose rather than a technical account of every doubtful mark.

The archivist asked what kind of object the output was meant to be. A convenient search layer could tolerate different conventions from a scholarly transcription used as evidence for an author’s exact wording. Hiding uncertainty might help a reader move through a page while making it harder to distinguish a clear reading from a plausible reconstruction. The project needed to state the role of the text before deciding how much confidence its presentation should imply.

A language model could favour a word that fitted the surrounding sentence. That contextual fit was useful information, but it was not the same as evidence that the pen strokes supported the word. An unusual technical term or a deliberate grammatical irregularity might be less predictable than a familiar phrase and nevertheless be what the writer had put on the page. Fluency was therefore not a universal test of transcription fidelity.

The team kept image references alongside text positions. Where the image itself was unclear, a human review could also remain uncertain. The workflow allowed a proposed reading, an uncertainty marker and an alternative account, instead of forcing every disputed location into a falsely final answer. Later revisions retained the basis and date of the change.

Evaluation sampled different handwriting styles and page conditions. An average score across easy pages did not describe performance on faded marginal notes. The team also distinguished recognition errors from disagreements about editorial conventions, such as whether an abbreviation should be expanded in the displayed version. A single total could otherwise count a deliberate presentation choice as though it were a failure to read a letter shape.

The archive ultimately offered a searchable layer connected with page images and a more carefully reviewed transcription where needed. It did not claim that retaining images made the text automatically correct. The connection made checking and correction possible. Readers could understand the text as an attributed, revisable representation of a particular source rather than a transparent replacement for it.

The project’s success lay partly in preserving the difference between assistance and evidence. Software could make a collection far easier to explore while the archive continued to show where a reading came from, which editorial decisions shaped it and what remained unresolved.

questions.prompt: What concern did the archivist raise about smooth output?
options: It could conceal the difference between a clear reading and a reconstruction.
It necessarily preserved every uncertain mark perfectly.
Readers could never benefit from searchable text.
The archive had no need to define the text’s purpose.
questions.explanation: A正确：顺畅显文可抹清晰与拟读界，须先定检索/证据用途。B不保；C可助检索；D需定义。

questions.prompt: Why is contextual plausibility insufficient for fidelity?
options: A writer can use only common grammatical phrases.
The image can never provide relevant evidence.
A plausible word may fit the sentence while failing to match the actual pen strokes.
Unusual terms must always be errors.
questions.explanation: C正确：语境合适不等笔画支持，罕术语或特语法可原作。A、D否认原文异样；B图像关键。

questions.prompt: What did the uncertainty workflow allow?
options: Every human review had to end in certainty.
Revisions were made without any recorded basis.
Image references were removed once text existed.
Proposed readings and alternatives could remain marked and later be revised traceably.
questions.explanation: D正确：疑可保拟读替读标记，后改留依据日期并连图。A不强定；B反；C留图位。

questions.prompt: Why separate editorial conventions from recognition errors?
options: All expanded abbreviations prove the software failed.
An intentional expansion of an abbreviation is different from misreading its letters.
Conventions never affect evaluation.
A single average necessarily describes every page condition.
questions.explanation: B正确：缩写展开是显示决策非必识字错，应分评价。A混同；C影响；D易页均不盖旧边注。

questions.prompt: What does retaining source-image links accomplish?
options: It enables checking and revision while keeping the representation’s provenance visible.
It guarantees no text can contain an error.
It makes uncertainty unnecessary.
It establishes fluency as the sole standard of accuracy.
questions.explanation: A正确：连图供核改归源非自动正确，保表述选择未定。B不保；C仍疑；D流畅非唯一准。

units.title: 六级阅读：通知实验中的分配与响应及碳抵消的额外性

materials.title: The Message That Was Sent but Not Read
materials.text:
A fictional product study randomly assigned eligible users to receive a reminder or receive no reminder during a defined period. The team wanted to learn whether offering the reminder affected completion of a task. Its first analysis compared only people who opened the message with everyone who did not open one. A manager described the difference as the experimental effect of sending the reminder.

The analyst pointed out that random assignment concerned the offered intervention, not the later choice to read it. People who opened the message might differ in attention, availability or motivation from those who did not. Restricting the comparison to openers could undo the protection provided by the original assignment. A recorded action after assignment was not automatically another randomised condition.

The team therefore retained an analysis based on the assigned groups for the stated question about offering the reminder. Delivery failures and unopened messages remained part of how that offer operated in practice. This estimate did not answer every question about what would happen if every person could be made to read the message. The two questions involved different interventions and required different supporting assumptions.

Measurement introduced another distinction. A device could report a message as displayed without establishing that its recipient had read or understood it. A later task completion could occur through another route. The study recorded the events with precise labels rather than treating sent, displayed, read and acted upon as four interchangeable names for one success.

The analyst also checked who had been eligible and included. A result from users with a particular device setting did not automatically describe all users of the service. Random allocation within a selected sample did not erase the consequences of how that sample had been defined. The report kept the internal comparison and its possible application elsewhere as related but separate issues.

The final account described the assigned-group result, the delivery process and the limitations of the behavioural measures. Opening patterns were still useful for understanding implementation and generating questions, but were not presented as if participants had been randomly assigned to be attentive.

The study thus replaced one appealing causal sentence with a more exact set of claims. It asked what had actually been assigned, what had been observed later and which outcome the comparison supported. Clear event definitions did not weaken the experiment. They made it possible to interpret the evidence without granting a later self-selected action the authority of the original randomisation.

questions.prompt: Why was comparing message openers with non-openers problematic as the experimental effect?
options: Opening and task completion were identical events by definition.
Randomisation had assigned every person to read attentively.
No users were assigned to a comparison group.
Opening was self-selected after assignment and could reflect other relevant differences.
questions.explanation: D正确：随机的是提醒机会，开信后选受动机可用等影响，筛开者破原保护。B未强读；C有无提醒组；A非同。

questions.prompt: What question did the assigned-group analysis address?
options: The effect of making every person understand the message perfectly.
The effect of offering the reminder under the implementation studied.
The universal effect on every possible service user.
The effect of motivation independently randomised after delivery.
questions.explanation: B正确：分配组估此实施条件offer，失败不读都属运作。A需另干预假设；C样本限；D动机未随机。

questions.prompt: Why distinguish displayed from read?
options: A device event does not necessarily establish a recipient’s attention or understanding.
The distinction makes every observation useless.
A displayed indicator directly measures comprehension.
Only the word sent has any measurable meaning.
questions.explanation: A正确：设备显示非人已读懂，事件需精标。C反；B仍用；D发送显示完成均可测不同。

questions.prompt: What does randomisation within eligible users not automatically establish?
options: A comparison between assigned groups.
The importance of keeping event definitions clear.
That the result applies unchanged to users excluded by the eligibility conditions.
The need to retain delivery failures.
questions.explanation: C正确：选样内随机不消纳入条件对外推影响。A、B、D非未建立而是设计支持或需做。

questions.prompt: How can opening patterns still be useful?
options: As proof that attention was randomly assigned.
As implementation evidence and a source of questions, with their self-selection made explicit.
As a substitute for knowing who was eligible.
As a guarantee all task completions resulted from reading.
questions.explanation: B正确：可助理解运作提问题但不能假随机注意。A错；C需样本；D完成可他路。

materials.title: A Reduction Compared with What?
materials.text:
A fictional climate-policy seminar examined a project that claimed to offset emissions by preserving a tract of land. Its presentation showed the carbon currently stored there and a certificate naming a quantity of avoided emissions. A student assumed that the stored total and the claimed offset were simply two measurements of the same thing.

The tutor separated a stock from a change relative to a counterfactual. Carbon already present was relevant to the project, but an offset claim concerned what would happen with the project compared with an appropriate account of what would happen without it. If the land would have remained protected anyway, continuing its existing state could be valuable without generating the same additional climate benefit claimed by the certificate.

The baseline was therefore not a photograph of an alternative world. It was an argued scenario supported by evidence and assumptions. A very pessimistic account of what would otherwise happen could enlarge a claimed difference. The seminar asked whether the scenario was credible, how uncertainty was handled and whether revisions could be traced. It did not treat a baseline as either directly observed truth or an unconstrained story chosen to maximise a number.

Activities could also shift beyond the project boundary. Preventing one use in one place might displace some of it elsewhere. That possibility did not prove that every project had no benefit, but it meant that a local account could miss relevant changes. The class connected the boundary with the causal claim rather than assuming that all consequences stopped at a mapped line.

Duration mattered too. A benefit vulnerable to later reversal differed from a permanent elimination of a source of emissions. The account needed to state the period considered and the arrangements for addressing a reversal. A certificate’s existence did not itself settle the durability of the underlying physical outcome.

Finally, the team distinguished an estimated project benefit from the accounting act of using that benefit against another entity’s emissions. The same claimed quantity should not silently support incompatible claims by multiple parties. An administrative record could help prevent such conflicts while still depending on the quality of the physical estimate beneath it.

The seminar’s conclusion was not that stored carbon or land protection lacked value. It was that a specific offset claim required a chain of comparisons and accounting decisions. Assessing that claim meant examining additionality, displacement, duration and attribution, rather than reading a large current stock as an automatically equivalent reduction elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Why is current stored carbon not automatically equal to an offset benefit?
options: All stored carbon disappears whenever measured.
A stock and a counterfactual difference are identical by definition.
The benefit depends on a change relative to a credible without-project scenario.
Land protection can never have value.
questions.explanation: C正确：抵消涉有项目与无项目差，不是当前存量直接等减排。A无据；B概念异；D保护可贵。

questions.prompt: How should a baseline be understood?
options: As an evidence-supported scenario whose assumptions and uncertainty require scrutiny.
As a number freely chosen to maximise the certificate.
As a directly photographed alternative world.
As proof that every project is ineffective.
questions.explanation: A正确：基线是论证情境，需可信证据假设不确定可追修。C不可直观另一世界；B任捏错；D不一概否。

questions.prompt: What concern is raised by displacement?
options: Every effect necessarily stops at the mapped line.
An activity prevented locally may shift elsewhere, affecting the broader causal claim.
It makes project boundaries irrelevant.
It proves all projects have zero benefit.
questions.explanation: B正确：局部阻活动可转界外，边界要合因果影响，非全零。A错；D过推；C界很相关。

questions.prompt: Why distinguish a certificate from durability?
options: A current stock guarantees permanent avoided emissions.
Certificates physically prevent every future reversal.
Duration is irrelevant to the claim.
An administrative record alone does not establish how long the physical benefit persists.
questions.explanation: D正确：证书不定物理持久，需时期及逆转安排。B不物理保；C时效要紧；A不可自动永久。

questions.prompt: Which account best reflects the conclusion?
options: All land protection is worthless unless carbon is sold.
A large stock automatically cancels any unrelated emissions.
A specific offset claim needs supported counterfactual, boundary, duration and attribution decisions.
Preventing conflicting accounting claims proves every physical estimate correct.
questions.explanation: C正确：需额外性位移期间归属链，存量不自动等他处减排。A不否保护值；B错误；D账无冲不保估真。

units.title: 六级阅读：档案中的缺席与检索回答的引文支持

materials.title: The Worker Missing from the Register
materials.text:
A fictional historian examined a workshop’s surviving payroll register. One person named in a later memoir did not appear in the pages available to the archive. A draft exhibition label concluded that the memoir must have invented the person’s employment. The historian asked what kind of absence the register could establish.

The surviving material did not cover every year. Some pages were damaged, and the register’s categories had changed over time. Certain kinds of temporary work might have been recorded elsewhere. These possibilities did not prove that the memoir was correct. They showed that an absent name in this particular record was not automatically equivalent to absence from the workshop’s entire history.

The historian reconstructed how the document had been produced. A payroll register was created for an administrative purpose, not to answer every later biographical question. Its fields reflected what the office needed to track. A person’s role might appear under an unfamiliar spelling, a household arrangement or a category that did not align with the memoir’s description. Searching required attention to those practices rather than matching one modern phrase against one column.

At the same time, the team resisted filling every gap with a preferred story. A claim could remain unconfirmed. The memoir had its own distance from the events, narrative purposes and possible mistakes. Contextualising the payroll did not make the later source immune to criticism. The task was to compare what each record could support, not to choose the more appealing account and explain away every difficulty.

The project also examined the path by which documents had survived. An archive containing mostly management papers could offer a rich account of official decisions while preserving fewer direct accounts from casual workers. The balance of surviving voices was itself historically informative, but it could not be treated as a transparent count of who had mattered in everyday life.

The final label stated that the available payroll had not confirmed the memoir’s account and explained the coverage problem. It identified further sources that might bear on the question, without presenting their future discovery as guaranteed. Readers could see both the negative result of the current search and the reason that result did not settle every larger claim.

Historical restraint here meant avoiding two opposite shortcuts. Silence in a source was not automatically proof that an event never occurred, and a gap was not permission to assert that it did. The strength of an argument depended on how document purpose, survival, search and independent evidence were connected to the precise proposition under examination.

questions.prompt: Why was the initial exhibition label too strong?
options: The available register’s coverage and categories did not make an absent name decisive proof of invented employment.
The memoir was guaranteed to be correct.
Every payroll page had survived intact.
Administrative records can never provide historical evidence.
questions.explanation: A正确：存页年类有界，缺名不直接证全史无工，需目的存续搜索。B仍可错；C有缺损；D可供证。

questions.prompt: Why reconstruct the register’s administrative purpose?
options: To make its categories universal for all later questions.
To prove every worker used one modern spelling.
To understand which activities and identities its recording practices might include or obscure.
To replace all source criticism with sympathy.
questions.explanation: C正确：原记录为办公，类拼写家庭等左右可见，需据其制作理解。A非普适；B拼写可异；D仍批两源。

questions.prompt: How does the historian treat gaps in the payroll?
options: As confirmation of any preferred narrative.
As proof that the memoir needs no scrutiny.
As evidence all archival work should stop.
As limits that can leave the claim unconfirmed without establishing its opposite.
questions.explanation: D正确：可以未证而非断反；空白不许填爱故事，回忆也批。A、B反；C还找他源。

questions.prompt: What can an archive dominated by management papers imply?
options: Only managers were historically significant.
The surviving record may reflect institutional preservation rather than the full distribution of lived experience.
Casual workers could not have existed.
The surviving voice balance exactly counts every worker.
questions.explanation: B正确：保存偏管理是制度史信息非生活重要性人口透明表。A、D、C皆把存留错当全史。

questions.prompt: What did the final label communicate?
options: The current search had not confirmed the account, and the limits of that negative finding were stated.
Employment was proved impossible in every year.
A future discovery was guaranteed to settle the claim.
The source gap itself established the memoir’s accuracy.
questions.explanation: A正确：可用工资册未证并明覆盖问题和他源可能，不保将发现。B过断；C未保；D空非正证。

materials.title: A Citation Beside a Confident Answer
materials.text:
A fictional research team tested an assistant that retrieved documents before composing an answer. Its output included links to several real passages in the supplied collection. A reviewer initially treated the presence of links as enough to establish that every sentence of the answer was supported.

The evaluation separated several questions. Did the cited document exist? Did the link identify the intended passage? Was that passage relevant to the topic? And did it actually support the specific claim to which the answer attached it? A reference could satisfy the first three checks while failing the fourth. A source discussing a treatment, for example, did not necessarily establish the particular outcome or population stated in a generated sentence.

Retrieval also had a coverage problem. The system selected a limited set of documents under its indexing and ranking arrangements. An answer saying that no evidence existed made a stronger claim than an account saying that none had been found in the searched collection. A missing result could reflect incomplete indexing, an unsuitable query or a genuinely absent source. The evaluation kept those possibilities separate where the evidence did not resolve them.

The team distinguished quotation from synthesis. A sentence combining information from several passages could be reasonable without appearing verbatim in any single one. It still needed a defensible connection between the sources and the conclusion. Conversely, copying a genuine sentence accurately did not guarantee that its original qualifications survived when it was placed in a new surrounding argument.

Versions mattered too. A cited page could have been revised after the answer was produced, or an older document could have been superseded in the relevant collection. The test retained the retrieved versions and the time of the answer so later checks would examine the evidence actually available rather than an imagined permanent web page.

The final assessment reported source existence, passage alignment, claim support and retrieval coverage as different aspects of performance. It did not infer that all unsupported statements were deliberate deception, nor did it excuse them because the links looked scholarly. The failure was defined in terms of the evidence the answer claimed to provide.

Retrieval made the assistant’s reasoning easier to examine when its references could be followed, but it did not automatically turn composition into verified knowledge. The useful interface showed what had been searched, where a claim came from and what qualification remained. A citation was an invitation to inspect a relationship between text and evidence, not a decorative guarantee that the relationship was sound.

questions.prompt: Why could a genuine relevant citation still fail the evaluation?
options: Its existence automatically proved every attached outcome.
It might not support the particular claim attached to it.
All synthesis required verbatim copying.
Every linked document was necessarily fabricated.
questions.explanation: B正确：真实定位相关可全满足仍不证特定人群结果命题。A错误；C综合不必逐字；D引文可真。

questions.prompt: What distinction concerns retrieval coverage?
options: No search result always proves no evidence anywhere.
Indexing can never affect an answer.
A query defines the entire possible world.
Failure to find evidence in a defined search is weaker than establishing universal absence.
questions.explanation: D正确：有限库检索无得非全域无证，可因索引查询或真缺。A、C过域；B索引要紧。

questions.prompt: How should synthesis be assessed?
options: It must be rejected unless every sentence appears verbatim in one source.
It needs no evidence when several links are shown.
The connection from source passages to the combined claim must be defensible.
Accurate copying automatically preserves all original qualifications.
questions.explanation: C正确：多源综合可非逐字，但推接需可辩；真抄也可能脱限定。A过严；B无证错；D不自动保。

questions.prompt: Why retain retrieved document versions?
options: To let later verification inspect the material actually available when the answer was produced.
To guarantee pages could never change.
To make all older evidence irrelevant by definition.
To replace claim support with publication dates alone.
questions.explanation: A正确：留当时检索版和答时，后核不拿变后页当永久原证。B页可修；C旧版有当时用；D仍核支撑。

questions.prompt: What is the passage’s view of retrieval-based answering?
options: Links automatically transform every composition into verified knowledge.
Traceable retrieval aids examination, while claim support and coverage still require checks.
Unsupported statements always prove intentional deception.
Scholarly formatting removes the need to inspect evidence.
questions.explanation: B正确：可追检索使可核但非全保证，支撑覆盖分项核。A全称错；C不推意图；D格式非证。

units.title: 六级阅读：导航辅助的认知分工与投资组合的预期和实现

materials.title: Remembering the Route or Reaching the Door
materials.text:
A fictional cognition study asked participants to reach an unfamiliar building. One group received step-by-step navigation, while another used a map they could consult as needed. Both groups often arrived successfully. A report draft concluded that the two methods had produced identical learning because the destination outcome was similar.

The research team separated completing the immediate task from building a representation of the surroundings. Turn-by-turn assistance could help a person arrive while reducing the need to select a route independently at each junction. That possibility did not imply that the assisted person’s memory had been damaged. It meant the task had distributed its demands differently between person and device.

A later test asked participants to recognise landmarks and describe relationships between locations without the same assistance. Those measures examined aspects of spatial learning that arrival alone did not reveal. The team kept the delay, instructions and available cues clear, since a memory test with different demands could produce a different comparison. No single score was assumed to measure everything that might reasonably be called knowing a place.

Individual goals also mattered. A visitor trying to reach an appointment promptly might value reliable assistance more than an opportunity to learn every surrounding street. A person intending to explore independently later might choose a different balance. The study did not convert an experimental comparison into a rule that every user should refuse navigation or always leave it on.

The device could also support active learning if its design or use encouraged attention to landmarks and the route’s structure. Assistance was not one fixed psychological treatment simply because every version appeared on a screen. The team described the specific prompts and interaction rather than treating the product category as a complete account of what participants had done.

The report considered selection as well. People who usually relied on navigation might already differ in experience or confidence from people who did not. A simple comparison of habitual users would not automatically identify the effect of the device. The experiment’s assigned conditions and its limits therefore remained distinct from broader observational patterns.

The final account described cognitive offloading as a redistribution of work under stated conditions. An external aid could improve immediate performance while changing which internal processes were exercised. Evaluating that change required naming the desired outcome, the later task and the user’s purpose. Reaching the right door and learning the surrounding network were related achievements, but neither could silently stand as a complete measure of the other.

questions.prompt: Why was identical arrival success insufficient to establish identical learning?
options: Arrival was never observed.
Both groups were guaranteed identical memories.
Immediate completion and internal knowledge of the surroundings were different outcomes.
The study defined learning as every possible future achievement.
questions.explanation: C正确：到达任务表现与空间表征学习分，抵门同不证后知同。B无保证；A有观察；D拒单分全知。

questions.prompt: How does the passage interpret reduced independent route decisions?
options: As a possible redistribution of task demands between person and aid.
As proof that the device permanently damaged memory.
As evidence that assisted people never saw landmarks.
As a guarantee that maps could not aid learning.
questions.explanation: A正确：分步助可少自主选路，属人机分工改变非损记忆证明。B极端；C未说从未；D图可学。

questions.prompt: Why state delay, instructions and cues in later tests?
options: They make every test identical by definition.
Different testing demands can examine different aspects of spatial learning.
They remove the need to identify the outcome.
They prove a single score covers all knowledge of a place.
questions.explanation: B正确：后测需求异可问不同学习侧，须明延时指令提示。A非同；C需目标；D单分非全。

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about user goals?
options: Every user must reject assistance.
Arriving promptly is never a reasonable aim.
Learning every street is always the sole objective.
The value of assistance can depend on whether immediate arrival or later independent exploration is the priority.
questions.explanation: D正确：约会快到与后自探可不同权衡，不推普开或关。A、B、C单一目标皆反文。

questions.prompt: Why is habitual use alone insufficient to identify the device’s effect?
options: Selection never matters in observational comparisons.
All users were randomly assigned their lifelong habits.
Users may already differ in experience or confidence before use.
The product category uniquely determines every interaction.
questions.explanation: C正确：惯用者既有经验自信可异，观察比较不自因果。B非随机生习；A选择有影响；D具体提示亦异。

materials.title: An Average Return Nobody Had Yet Received
materials.text:
A fictional finance class compared two portfolios using a model of future returns. One had a higher expected return and greater exposure to particular risks. A student described the expected figure as the amount the investor was guaranteed to receive, then argued that combining several assets must remove the uncertainty completely.

The tutor explained that an expectation summarised outcomes under a stated probability model. It was not a payment promise or the single outcome that every investor would realise. A realised return belonged to a particular period and set of events. Even a model judged useful could produce an expectation that differed from the next observed result without that difference alone settling whether the model had been well specified.

Diversification concerned how asset returns moved together. Combining exposures could reduce some risks when their fluctuations did not coincide perfectly. It did not automatically remove risks shared across the portfolio. Counting a large number of holdings was therefore not enough to show that their underlying exposures were diverse. Several different names could still depend strongly on the same economic conditions.

The class distinguished risk capacity from a simple preference for a larger headline number. An investor needing funds soon could face a different problem from one able to tolerate a long uncertain interval. The model did not determine those needs merely by drawing a smooth curve of available portfolios. A recommendation required a connection between the modelled trade-offs and the actual purpose.

Measurement choices also mattered. A return before fees was different from what remained after the specified costs. A nominal increase did not by itself describe a change in purchasing power when prices changed. The class kept period, fees and inflation treatment attached to the comparison rather than treating every percentage as the same quantity.

Past results supplied evidence but did not guarantee that the same relationships would persist. A correlation estimated over one interval could differ in another, especially when the conditions generating returns changed. The tutor retained uncertainty about the estimates as well as uncertainty about future outcomes. A calculation could be exact given its inputs while those inputs remained imperfect guides to the future.

The final exercise was consequently an assessment of a modelled choice, not a promise of profit. Students had to state what was expected, which risks diversification could address and which conditions made the comparison relevant. The most informative answer connected return, dependence, costs and horizon, rather than declaring one portfolio universally best because its expected figure was largest.

questions.prompt: What error did the student make about expected return?
options: An expectation can never be computed.
Expected and realised were explicitly different in the student’s claim.
Every model guaranteed the same outcome.
A model-based average was treated as a guaranteed realised payment.
questions.explanation: D正确：模型期望非承诺或人人实现额，学生混同。A可算；C模型非保同；B他恰混未分。

questions.prompt: When can several holdings fail to provide broad diversification?
options: Their printed names are all different.
They share strong underlying exposures despite having different names.
No asset has any uncertainty.
The portfolio’s holdings are recorded clearly.
questions.explanation: B正确：多名可同经济条件风险，高共动不自动消共同风险。A不同名本身非关键；C无此设；D清记不妨分散。

questions.prompt: Why consider an investor’s horizon and needs?
options: The practical suitability of a trade-off depends on the purpose and ability to bear uncertainty.
Only the largest expected number can matter.
Near-term needs and long-term tolerance are always identical.
A smooth model curve reveals every personal need.
questions.explanation: A正确：近期用钱与长持承受异，模型曲线不定需求，须连接目的。D反；B单一指标；C异。

questions.prompt: Why retain fee and inflation treatment with a percentage?
options: A nominal gain always guarantees equal real gain.
All percentages have identical economic meaning.
Before-cost, after-cost and purchasing-power measures answer different questions.
Fees can never affect realised proceeds.
questions.explanation: C正确：费前费后及名义购买力不同量，需时期处理。B混同；A通胀可改；D费用影响净得。

questions.prompt: How should an exact portfolio calculation be interpreted?
options: As conditional on inputs whose estimation and future relevance may remain uncertain.
As proof that estimated inputs and future relationships are certain.
As a guarantee that one historical correlation never changes.
As a universal recommendation independent of costs and horizon.
questions.explanation: A正确：给定输入可精算但输入估计及未来机制仍疑。B错；C相关可变；D要成本目的期限。
